Create spatial cross-validation folds

Source: R/cross-validation.R
make_folds.Rd

Builds train/test splits by random k-fold, spatial block k-fold, leave-location-out, buffered leave-one-out, nearest-neighbour distance matching (NNDM) leave-one-out or its k-fold version (kNNDM).

Usage

make_folds(
  points_sf,
  k,
  method = c("random_kfold", "block_kfold", "buffered_loo", "leave_location_out", "nndm",
    "knndm"),
  seed = NULL,
  block_nx = NULL,
  block_ny = NULL,
  block_multiplier = 3,
  block_size = NULL,
  auto_range = FALSE,
  range_frac = 1,
  response_var = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  prediction_points = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  boundary = NULL,
  buffer = NULL,
  min_train = 0.5,
  phi = NULL,
  drop_empty_blocks = TRUE,
  blocks = NULL,
  balance_tol = 3,
  max_test = NULL
)

Arguments

points_sf

An sf object. Any Z or M dimension is dropped before folding: sf::st_distance() uses every coordinate dimension, so an XYZ layer would otherwise have elevation folded into every buffer, block and neighbour distance. CRS-less points are aligned to a boundary or prediction_points that carries a CRS. They are reprojected when the coordinates look like lon/lat and otherwise stamped without reprojection, with a warning either way.

k

Integer; number of folds. Must be a single whole number >= 1, and is required except for the two leave-one-out methods. A fraction, NA or a vector is an error, because a non-integer used to truncate silently and leave the last rows in no test set at all. Not every method honours it. "buffered_loo" and "nndm" are leave-one-out schemes and always return one fold per held-out point (k = n, or max_test when that is given) regardless of what was asked for; "block_kfold" lowers it when the grid yields fewer than k non-empty blocks, and "leave_location_out" lowers it when there are fewer than k distinct groups. "random_kfold" and "knndm" lower it only when the layer has fewer than k rows. k = 1 is raised to 2 by "random_kfold", "block_kfold", "leave_location_out" and "knndm", since one fold has no training set. Read the k element of the returned list, and do not assume the requested value; params$k_requested keeps the value asked for. Returning fewer folds than asked raises a warning of class "spatialkit_k_reduced", whose message gives both counts, the reason and a setting that works; the condition carries them as k_requested and k, so tryCatch(spatialkit_k_reduced = ) or withCallingHandlers() can act on it without reading the text. (Before this version a reduction was a log line only.)

method

One of "random_kfold", "block_kfold", "buffered_loo", "leave_location_out", "nndm" or "knndm". See Details for what each one does and when it is appropriate.

seed

Optional integer RNG seed. "nndm" is deterministic and reads it only to draw the max_test subset; "buffered_loo" likewise. "knndm" uses it for the random partition among its candidates, for ties in the packing, and above 4,000 points for the k-means starts, so its folds are reproducible only with a seed.

block_nx, block_ny

Optional grid dimensions for block_kfold, each a single whole number >= 1. Give both, or give one and the other is derived from the extent's aspect ratio so that the blocks are roughly square. Ignored when block_size or auto_range override them.

block_multiplier

A single positive number, default 3. When neither block_size nor block_nx/block_ny is given, the automatic grid aims for block_multiplier * k blocks over the extent (aspect-preserving), so each fold holds out about block_multiplier blocks. An extent more than about block_multiplier * k times as wide as it is tall (or as tall as it is wide) gets a single row (or column) of that many blocks. With 1, every fold is one contiguous region and the score depends heavily on which region each fold happened to get; with many, the blocks shrink towards single points and the scheme drifts back towards random k-fold. 3 is a compromise between those two, not a published constant. The block size that matters for leakage is the autocorrelation range, which is what block_size and auto_range control.

block_size

Optional positive numeric minimum block edge length, in the units of the CRS the folds are built in. Takes precedence over block_nx/block_ny and block_multiplier. When supplied, a whole number of blocks is fitted across each axis of the extent: as many as leave every block at least this long on that axis. On an axis at least as long as block_size the blocks built are therefore from one to just under two times this size. An axis shorter than block_size cannot hold a block that long: a single row or column spans it, and its blocks are as long as the extent on that axis, which is less than the size asked (a 39.8 km by 5 km extent with block_size = 10000 gets three blocks 13.3 km wide and 5 km tall). params$block_width and params$block_height record what was built. A size that leaves fewer than k blocks holding points returns that many folds, with a warning (see k); one that leaves a single block is an error. Both name the largest size that still gives k folds.

Which CRS that is depends on the input. Projected input is used as it stands, so block_size is in your own CRS's units. Geographic (lon/lat) input is projected first by ensure_projected(), which picks a local UTM zone or, at wide extents, an equal-area projection. That is a CRS you did not choose, whose units are metres but whose identity varies with the data. block_size is then interpreted in that CRS. The CRS actually used is recorded in params$crs of the returned list; project the data yourself before calling if you want to fix the units in advance.

A block_size in the wrong unit asks for an enormous grid, so a request above 1,000,000 blocks is refused with an error naming the grid dimensions, the extent and the CRS's units.

auto_range

Logical. If TRUE, the spatial autocorrelation range is estimated via estimate_sac_range() (the omnidirectional, all-pairs range; the directional ranges it also fits are a diagnostic only, so on a field known to be anisotropic pass block_size = max(attr(r, "directional_fitted"), na.rm = TRUE) yourself after checking attr(r, "directional_status"), see estimate_sac_range) and used as the minimum block_size. Requires response_var. An explicit block_size takes precedence. Default FALSE. Sizing blocks from the autocorrelation range is the recommendation of Roberts et al. (2017) and what blockCV (Valavi et al. 2019) automates. blockCV takes the fitted variogram's range parameter as the block size, whereas this uses the effective range estimate_sac_range() returns (three times that parameter for an exponential fit), so its blocks are larger than blockCV's from the same variogram. When no range is identified, the geometric grid is used instead, with a warning that gives the reason. Range-sized blocks do not fit every layout. On a square extent at k = 5 a range up to a third of the side gives five folds; up to half, a 2 x 2 grid and four folds, returned with the "spatialkit_k_reduced" warning; and above half the extent in both directions there is room for a single block, and make_folds() stops with an error naming the size, rather than return one fold with an empty training set. The warning and the error name the largest block size that still gives k folds on this layout and how far below the range it is; method = "nndm" is the design that does not depend on a block size. The message printed when the range is used states the grid and the block size built.

range_frac

Passed through to estimate_sac_range() when auto_range = TRUE. A fitted range beyond the longest lag the empirical variogram was fitted over is rejected as unidentified, and block sizing falls back to geometry (with a warning). A range within that bound can still be too wide for two blocks; see auto_range. Default 1.0.

response_var

Character(1) response column name. Required when auto_range = TRUE. For "block_kfold" a name that is not a column of points_sf is an error, whether or not auto_range is set: with it off the response still feeds the leakage warning, which a misspelt name would silently disable.

group_var

Character(1) naming a column of points_sf that identifies the location each observation belongs to. Required for method = "leave_location_out", which keeps every observation from a location together in the same fold. Repeated measurements at the same site otherwise get split across folds, and the model is scored partly on sites it has already seen, which random k-fold reports as excellent performance.

prediction_points

Optional sf layer of the locations you actually intend to predict onto. Required for method = "nndm" and method = "knndm". The grid from predict_surface() is the natural choice; a non-POINT layer (grid cells, polygons) is reduced to representative points first, so the target distances are point-to-point. A point-to-polygon distance is zero for every cell that contains a training point, which pulls the target distribution towards zero and degenerates the CV towards plain leave-one-out.

predictor_vars

Optional character vector of predictor column names. Passed to estimate_sac_range() for residual variogram estimation.

boundary

Optional polygonal sf/sfc for block_kfold. The grid is clipped to it; a cell that the boundary only touches at a corner or along an edge is not a block. A boundary without a CRS is brought into the points' CRS: reprojected from EPSG:4326 when its coordinates look like lon/lat, otherwise stamped, with a warning either way. The same goes for prediction_points and blocks.

buffer

For "buffered_loo": a single positive number, the distance within which the held-out point's neighbours are excluded from its training set. Like block_size it is in the units of the CRS the folds are built in (params$crs), which for geographic (lon/lat) input is the metre CRS ensure_projected() chooses: 0.1 means 0.1 m, not 0.1 degrees. A buffer that excludes no neighbour from any fold makes the scheme plain leave-one-out, and is warned about.

min_train

For method = "nndm": the smallest fraction of the data any fold's training set may be reduced to by neighbour exclusion. Default 0.5, as in CAST::nndm(). Where it binds, the distance matching stops short and the cross-validation stays optimistic; see Details. For method = "knndm": the smallest fraction of the data a fold may leave for training, so a candidate whose largest fold holds more than 1 - min_train of the rows is set aside (the maxp = 0.5 of CAST::knndm() is min_train = 0.5). Equal folds leave 1 - 1/k of the data, so a value above that is an error.

phi

For method = "nndm": the distance up to which the two nearest-neighbour distance distributions are matched, in the CRS the folds are built in. Matching is attempted only while a held-out point's nearest-neighbour distance is at most phi; the exclusion that takes it past phi is the last one, so a realised distance can exceed phi by up to one neighbour step, as in CAST::nndm(). In Mila et al. (2022), and in CAST::nndm(), \(\phi\) is the autocorrelation range of the outcome: beyond it observations are effectively independent, so matching is unnecessary. estimate_sac_range() gives such a value. Default NULL = the largest prediction-to-training distance, which matches everywhere (CAST's phi = "max").

drop_empty_blocks

Logical. Default TRUE. With FALSE the blocks that hold no point are kept and packed into folds too, but k is still lowered to the number of blocks that hold points, so no fold is left without test points.

blocks

Optional polygon layer (sf or sfc, POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON, at least two features) to use as the blocks of "block_kfold" in place of the grid this function would otherwise build: the $cells of a build_tessellation() result, hexagons, watersheds, administrative units, the $blocks of blockCV::cv_spatial(). Each point takes the block that contains it, and the blocks are then assigned to folds exactly as grid cells are. block_size, block_nx/block_ny, block_multiplier and boundary have nothing to act on and are ignored (logged); auto_range only compares the estimated range against the blocks. See Supplied blocks below for the CRS, overlap and coverage rules. An error for any other method.

balance_tol

A number of at least 1, default 3. For "block_kfold": the ratio of the largest fold's point count to the smallest's above which the folds are reported as imbalanced, with a warning (an R condition, also logged) that names both counts. Inf disables the check. The value is the tolerance of a check, not a target the packing aims for: see Fold balance below for what the packing can and cannot do. params$balance_ratio carries the ratio achieved. For "knndm" it is a limit and not a check: a candidate whose largest fold holds more than balance_tol times the points of its smallest is set aside, so the folds returned are always within it.

max_test

For "buffered_loo" and "nndm": optional whole number of at least 2. Folds are built for a random subset of that many held-out points (drawn under seed), and every row stays available for training, so each fold returned is the fold the full design has for that point. The model is then refitted max_test times and not n times, and the folds hold 4 * n * max_test bytes of row indices in place of 4 * n^2, which lets "buffered_loo" run on layers its storage limit otherwise refuses. It does not lift the 5,000-row limit of "nndm", whose cost is the matching itself; for that there is "knndm". Rows that are not held out have NA in assignment$fold. For "nndm" the matching still runs over all n points and params describes all of them. area_of_applicability() needs every training row in a test fold and refuses a subset. Default NULL: every point is held out once. An error for the k-fold methods, whose number of folds is k.

Value

A list with method, k, folds, assignment, params. The train/test elements of each fold contain ..row_id values (equal to row positions when the input has no pre-existing ..row_id column), consistent with the assignment tibble. The returned k is the number of folds actually built, which is not always the k that was requested (see the k argument above), and length(folds) always matches it.

For "block_kfold" the block design is returned with the folds. assignment has a third column, block_id: the block each point fell in, numbered as the rows of params$blocks, an sf layer of the block polygons in the CRS the folds were built in. Those rows are not the rows of the layer the blocks came from: drop_empty_blocks = TRUE (the default) removes the blocks that hold no point and renumbers the rest, so with supplied blocks a nine-polygon layer of which three are empty comes back as six rows numbered 1 to 6. params$blocks$source_row is the row each one came from in that original layer (a grid cell's index in the full grid_nx by grid_ny grid, or the row of the blocks argument), so blocks[params$blocks$source_row, ] recovers them with their own columns and in their own order. It runs from 1 to params$n_blocks and is the identity when nothing was dropped. For a grid params$n_blocks is grid_nx * grid_ny, the cells a boundary clips away included, and params$blocks_used is the number of blocks returned. params$block_sizes is the number of points in each block, indexed by block_id (zeros are empty blocks that drop_empty_blocks = FALSE kept), and params$fold_blocks is a list with one integer vector per fold naming the blocks packed into it. Between them the folds account for every block exactly once, empty ones included, so a fold's territory on the map is all of its blocks and not merely the ones that happen to hold points. So table(assignment$fold) can be traced back to the blocks it is made of, a fold can be seen to be one contiguous region or several, and the blocks can be drawn over the data (plot_folds() does so).

For "block_kfold", params carries a params$blocks_supplied that says whether the blocks came from blocks or from a grid built here, and params$boundary_supplied whether a boundary was given. params$block_width and params$block_height are the width and height of the grid cells built, before any clipping to a boundary (NA for supplied blocks); they are what block_size turned into: at least that size on an axis long enough to hold it, and the whole extent on an axis that is not (see block_size). Every method's params carries params$k_requested, the k that was asked for (NA when none was given), beside the k returned, and params$row_probe, a small sample of row IDs and coordinates that every cv_*() compares against the data it is handed, so folds built from a different layer of the same size are refused, never applied silently.

For "knndm", params carries chosen ("random" or "clusters"), n_clusters (the number of clusters packed into the folds; NA for the random partition), clustering ("ward" or "kmeans+ward"; NA when no cluster count was tried), candidates (a data frame with one row per candidate, the random partition first: candidate, n_clusters, largest_fold, balance_ratio, admissible and W, which is NA for a candidate set aside), wasserstein, wasserstein_random and wasserstein_loo (the Wasserstein distance to the target of the folds returned, of the random partition among the candidates and of plain leave-one-out, in distance units), fold_sizes, balance_ratio, target_distances and realised_distances (one per prediction point, and one per row: its distance to the nearest point of another fold) with their medians and means, and the diagnostics "nndm" reports under the same names: max_ecdf_excess, max_ecdf_deficit, loo_ecdf_deficit, ecdf_deficit_tol, target_separated and target_out_of_reach, with short_of_target for the opposite case (see Details).

With max_test, "buffered_loo" and "nndm" return that many folds, assignment$fold is NA for the rows not held out, and params$max_test records the value.

For the methods that work in projected space, params also carries a crs element naming the CRS the folds were built in (an "EPSG:code" string where there is one, otherwise the CRS's input definition). Every length in params (block_size, sac_range, buffer, median_buffer) is in that CRS's units, which for geographic input is a CRS ensure_projected() chose for you, and not one you passed.

Rows whose geometry is empty or has non-finite coordinates are dropped before folding, with a logged warning naming the count; they appear in no fold and in no assignment row.

Details

For block_kfold, the default grid sizing is purely geometric and unrelated to the autocorrelation range of the data. When blocks are smaller than the autocorrelation range, spatially correlated observations leak across folds and CV metrics become optimistic. Use block_size to set a minimum block edge length (in CRS units), or set auto_range = TRUE to estimate the range from an empirical variogram and enforce it automatically. When a response is given and the blocks come out smaller than the estimated range, the warning says what range-sized blocks would yield on this layout before recommending them: the setting and the grid it builds when that gives k folds, and otherwise how many folds it gives (or that it leaves a single block), the largest block size that still gives k folds, and method = "nndm" as the design that needs no block size.

Fold methods. "random_kfold" ignores geography entirely and will overstate performance on autocorrelated data. "block_kfold" separates folds geographically. "buffered_loo" holds out one point at a time and excludes everything within a fixed buffer.

"leave_location_out" groups by group_var, so all observations from a location share a fold.

"nndm" implements the distance-matching principle of Milà et al. (2022): it sizes the exclusion around each held-out point, with no arbitrary buffer, so that the resulting training-to-test distance distribution approaches the distribution of distances from your actual prediction locations to the training data.

The procedure is the paper's, and it is deterministic. Let \(G_{ij}\) be the empirical distribution of prediction-to-nearest-training distances and \(G_j^*\) the distribution of each held-out point's nearest remaining training point. Starting from plain leave-one-out, the point with the smallest \(G_j^*\) at which the realised distribution exceeds the target (\(G_j^*(r) > G_{ij}(r)\)) has its nearest training neighbour removed, and this repeats until no such point remains, subject to two limits: a point is matched only while its nearest-neighbour distance is at most phi (default: the largest prediction distance, since a training point already further than every prediction distance has nothing to match), so the exclusion that takes it past phi is its last and a realised distance can exceed phi by up to one neighbour step; and no fold's training set is stripped below min_train of the data.

It differs from CAST::nndm() in two details, so the folds agree closely with CAST's but not exactly. The removal rule is strict: a neighbour is removed whenever the realised distribution exceeds the target, whereas CAST removes one only while the realised distribution, less the point about to move, is still at or above the target. The rule here therefore removes up to one point more per distance value (a few percent more removals in all on clustered layouts), erring on the pessimistic side. And ties in \(G_j^*\) are broken by the points' coordinates, not by their row index as in CAST, so the folds do not depend on the order of the rows.

Where neither limit binds, the realised distribution of nearest-neighbour distances is then never shorter than the target: \(G_j^*(r) \le G_{ij}(r)\) up to the granularity of the neighbour distances, which is the property the method exists to deliver. It is a statement about the distance to the one nearest training point. A learner that draws on several neighbours (a forest, a k-nearest-neighbour mean, a kriging neighbourhood) also depends on how far the second and later neighbours are, which NNDM does not match, so on clustered samples its cross-validated error can still read low with the nearest-neighbour distances matched exactly. Beyond phi no matching is attempted, by design. min_train is different: when the prediction locations lie further from the samples than a fold can be made to hold out (clustered samples and a prediction domain well beyond them, the layout NNDM is meant for), it stops the matching early and the realised distances stay too short. params$n_at_min_train counts the folds that were held at the floor while still closer than the target allows, and make_folds() warns when that leaves more than one point's worth of excess at or below phi. Lower min_train to match further, or read the cross-validated score as an upper bound on performance at the prediction locations.

The match has a second side. params$max_ecdf_deficit is the largest amount by which the target distribution runs above the realised one, the mirror of params$max_ecdf_excess: the share of prediction points within some distance of the data that the folds do not reproduce. Part of it is the granularity of the matching. Excluding a neighbour moves a held-out point out to its next remaining neighbour, and on clustered samples that can be the next cluster, well past the prediction distances.

The other part no setting reaches. Excluding neighbours can only lengthen a held-out distance, so when the prediction points sit nearer to the data than the samples sit to each other (prediction points among the samples, or a regular sample predicted between its nodes) the folds returned are plain leave-one-out and are still farther from their training data than the prediction points are. The cross-validated error is then pessimistic for those locations: an upper bound on the error there. params$loo_ecdf_deficit is the largest amount by which the target distribution runs above that of plain leave-one-out. When it exceeds params$ecdf_deficit_tol, three times \(\sqrt{1/n + 1/m}\) for \(n\) folds and \(m\) prediction points (about three times the chance difference between two samples of one distribution), make_folds() raises a warning of class "spatialkit_nndm_out_of_reach" and sets params$target_out_of_reach to TRUE.

On small samples no deficit can exceed that tolerance. A deficit is a difference of two shares, so it is at most 1, and the tolerance is 1 or more whenever \(nm/(n+m) \le 9\): for nine folds or fewer whatever the number of prediction points, and for up to eighteen folds with as many prediction points. There the same warning is raised in one case only, complete separation: every prediction point nearer to the data than any sample is to its nearest other sample (a deficit of exactly 1), provided the two sets are large enough for that ordering to mean something, which is taken as choose(n + m, n) >= 1000 ways of interleaving them (17 prediction points for 3 folds, 7 for 6 folds, 4 for 12 folds). params$target_separated records the ordering whether or not it was enough to warn, and the warning's condition carries it as separated. With very few samples it can hold for a grid over the samples' own extent, because a few points hug the box they span; the folds are then farther than the grid all the same. A partial shortfall on such a sample (most prediction points nearer than leave-one-out reaches, not all) is not warned about: the tolerance is 1 or more at these sizes, which no difference of shares exceeds, so only complete separation can be reported. Compare params$target_median with params$realised_median.

params$wasserstein is the Wasserstein distance between the target and realised distributions, in distance units, and params$wasserstein_loo the same for plain leave-one-out: equal when nothing was excluded, smaller when the matching helped.

kNNDM. "knndm" is the k-fold version of that idea (Linnenbrink et al. 2024): k folds, and so k model fits, whose held-out distances are as close to the same target as a set of candidates allows. It has no row limit, and is the method to use above the 5,000 rows "nndm" takes or when a model is too costly to refit once per point. It is not an equal of NNDM below that: a fold design has far fewer degrees of freedom than one exclusion set per point, so the match is coarser.

The candidates are a random k-fold partition (the one "random_kfold" builds with the same seed) and, for each of up to 50 cluster counts spaced evenly on the log scale from k to one fewer than the number of distinct locations, the samples clustered on their coordinates and the clusters merged into k folds. Few large clusters give folds that are whole regions, far from their training data; many small ones approach the random partition. Up to 4,000 points the clustering is Ward's (stats::hclust(method = "ward.D2")), cut at each count. Above that, where the n by n distance matrix it needs is no longer affordable, k-means first reduces the samples to 4,000 groups (Lloyd's algorithm from random sample locations, at most ten passes) and Ward's method is continued from those groups; a count above 4,000 is a k-means run of its own. params$clustering says which ("ward" or "kmeans+ward"). Clusters are merged by the packing "block_kfold" uses for its blocks, largest first and each to the fold with the fewest points so far (see Fold balance). CAST::knndm() merges clusters by a rule of its own, which this was not checked against, so the folds are not expected to equal CAST's.

Each candidate is scored by the Wasserstein distance \(W\) between its held-out distances (each point's distance to the nearest point of another fold) and the target distances, and the smallest \(W\) is returned. A candidate is set aside without being scored when its largest fold leaves less than min_train of the rows for training or holds more than balance_tol times the points of its smallest; the random partition is always kept. So params$wasserstein is never above params$wasserstein_random, the \(W\) of that random partition, and params$candidates lists every candidate with its cluster count, fold sizes and \(W\). params$chosen is "random" when no clustering came closer, which is the right answer for samples spread evenly over the prediction area.

Read \(W\) against the mean target distance. On 400 points in 12 clusters predicted onto a grid over their extent (12 draws, 5 and 10 folds) the folds returned had \(W\) at 0.32 of the mean target distance, against 0.70 to 0.72 for a random partition and 0.01 for "nndm". A 5-nearest-neighbour learner scored 9 to 11 percent high on them, where random folds scored 23 to 25 percent low and "nndm" 6 percent low. On 2,000 points in 40 clusters of unequal size the ratio was 0.07 to 0.10, against 0.56 to 0.59 for a random partition and 0.003 to 0.006 for "nndm"; on 30,000 points of that layout it was 0.11 to 0.15, and on 100,000 points 0.27. So the method removes most of the mismatch of a random partition and leaves more of it than NNDM does, in either direction: \(W\) has no sign. On 400 evenly spread points the random partition or one close to it came back and the two scored alike (3.3 and 3.5 percent high). With few folds a random partition is itself farther than the target, since each fold trains on 1 - 1/k of the points: at k = 2 on evenly spread points the mean held-out distance was 9 to 53 percent above the target mean (60 draws of 100 to 1,000 points), and no candidate is nearer.

Construction took 2 s at 8,000 points and 10 s at 30,000 with ten folds (37 s at 100,000) with FNN installed, and three to four times that without it; it grows with the number of folds.

Two cases are warned about, each with a condition class. When the prediction points sit nearer to the data than a sample is to its nearest other sample, no fold design reaches them, since a held-out point is never nearer to its training data than that; the test is the one "nndm" applies, the warning has the same class, "spatialkit_nndm_out_of_reach", and what comes back is the random partition or a candidate as fine as one. In the other direction, the closest candidate can still be short of the target: prediction points well beyond the samples lie farther from the data than k folds of those samples can be held apart. When the mean held-out distance of the folds returned is below the mean target distance by more than a quarter of it and by at least half of \(W\) (the test fold_separation() words as "closer"), make_folds() raises a warning of class "spatialkit_knndm_short_of_target" and sets params$short_of_target: the cross-validated error then tends to read low for those locations. Fewer folds hold out larger regions. Short of either warning the folds can still differ from the target at some distances; params$max_ecdf_excess and params$max_ecdf_deficit give the largest difference each way, and fold_separation() reads the folds against the same prediction points fold by fold.

An earlier version of this package drew one random radius per point from \(G_{ij}\) and excluded up to the order statistic closest to it, which rounds down half the time: on a two-cluster layout the realised distribution exceeded the target by up to 0.17 (13% of folds had a nearest training point within 50 m against a target of 9%), an optimistic cross-validation. params$max_ecdf_excess reports the largest remaining excess; compare params$target_median with params$realised_median as well.

Supplied blocks

A polygon layer passed as blocks is aligned to the points the way boundary is: CRS-less points are aligned to blocks that carry a CRS (reprojected if they look like lon/lat, otherwise stamped, warning either way), and the blocks are then brought into the CRS the folds are built in. A point inside more than one block is given the first (lowest row) that contains it, as for a point on the shared edge of two grid cells. When the blocks that caught such a point share area instead of an edge, the layer overlaps and is not a partition, and this is warned about. A point inside no block is assigned to the nearest one, by distance to the polygon itself, and the count of such points is warned about, unless they sit within a millionth of the extent of a block, which is an edge that reprojection or clipping moved by a rounding error. Blocks that hold no point are dropped when drop_empty_blocks = TRUE, and k is lowered to the number of blocks that hold points when that is smaller. params$n_blocks is the number of blocks before empties were dropped, params$blocks_used the number after (so with drop_empty_blocks = FALSE the two are equal, and sum(params$block_sizes > 0) is how many of them hold points), params$grid_nx and params$grid_ny are NA, and params$block_scale is the median over blocks that hold points of the side of the square with the block's area. That is the length compared against the autocorrelation range for the leakage warning, since a polygon has no single edge length.

The connection to the rest of the package is build_tessellation(): every shape it builds can be a block design here, including Voronoi cells around get_voronoi_seeds(method = "kmeans") seeds, which adapt to the density of the points.

Fold balance

"block_kfold" and "knndm" balance the number of points per fold, and they do so by packing: blocks (for "knndm", clusters of the samples) are taken largest first and each goes to the fold with the fewest points so far, ties broken at random. This is the longest-processing-time rule for multiway partitioning. Measured against the optimum by enumeration (two folds, up to ten blocks, heavy-tailed block sizes) it is optimal in 72 percent of cases and within two points of optimal on average; a local search with 30 random restarts moved the largest-to-smallest ratio by 0.004 on average and never brought a packing above the 3:1 tolerance below it. An imbalance past the tolerance is therefore in the points per block, which no assignment of blocks to folds can even out, and this function offers no search over packings. The remedy is the block design: smaller blocks, or blocks that adapt to the density of the points passed through blocks. On clustered layouts where the geometric grid exceeded 3:1 in 22 percent of cases (median ratio 1.8, worst 6.3), Voronoi cells around 15 k-means seeds never exceeded 1.3 (median 1.09). Density-adaptive blocks are smaller where points are dense, so check params$block_scale against the autocorrelation range as you would a grid.

"knndm" chooses its clusters, so for it balance_tol is a limit: a clustering whose packing exceeds it is not a candidate, and the folds returned are within it (params$fold_sizes, params$balance_ratio).

The other methods do not balance point counts. "random_kfold" is balanced by construction (fold sizes differ by at most one); "buffered_loo" and "nndm" hold out one point per fold; "leave_location_out" gives each fold the same number of locations (to within one), so folds differ by as much as the locations' sizes do.

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(30, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(30, 0, 1000)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
folds <- make_folds(pts, k = 3, method = "block_kfold", seed = 42)
folds$assignment          # fold and block membership per row
#> # A tibble: 30 × 3
#>    row_id  fold block_id
#>     <int> <int>    <int>
#>  1      1     1        4
#>  2      2     3        8
#>  3      3     1        5
#>  4      4     2        3
#>  5      5     3        7
#>  6      6     2        9
#>  7      7     2        9
#>  8      8     3        2
#>  9      9     3        8
#> 10     10     1        4
#> # ℹ 20 more rows
lengths(folds$folds[[1]]) # train/test row-ID splits
#> train  test 
#>    20    10 
folds$params$block_sizes  # points per block; params$fold_blocks packs them
#> [1] 2 2 2 3 5 3 4 4 5

# Buffered leave-one-out: neighbours within 100 units excluded from training
loo <- make_folds(pts, k = 1, method = "buffered_loo", buffer = 100)

# Three folds matched to the distances from a prediction grid to the data
grid <- st_make_grid(pts, n = c(10, 10), what = "centers")
km <- make_folds(pts, k = 3, method = "knndm", prediction_points = grid,
                 seed = 42)
km$params[c("chosen", "n_clusters", "wasserstein", "wasserstein_random")]
#> $chosen
#> [1] "random"
#> 
#> $n_clusters
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $wasserstein
#> [1] 20.95776
#> 
#> $wasserstein_random
#> [1] 20.95776
#>
